period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem Aloud and Activating Prior Knowledge

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.16): paired oral — who inspires you to do your best?
Let us read (p.16): picture-pairs discussion — what can we learn from nature?

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading oral prompt from 'Let us read' (p.16): ask students who or what inspires them to do their best. Take two or three quick responses to warm up the room.

Move to the paired picture activity from 'Let us read' (p.16): show the six images (honeybee hive, spider web, geese, weaver bird, ants, apple tree) and ask pairs what lesson each offers. Brief whole-class share-out follows.

Teacher reads the full poem 'Try Again' aloud (pp.16–18) at an unhurried pace while students follow in their books. Pause briefly at the end of each stanza to let the imagery settle; invite students to note any word or line that strikes them.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading images of ants, spiders and geese are deliberately chosen to echo the poem's central metaphor of persistent effort in nature. Students who recognise the spider connection early may read the poem with sharper attention to the spider's nine attempts. A self-study pointer: the pictures activity asks students to share observations with classmates — pairs who did not finish can note remaining images on their own.
materials: Textbook pp.16–18 (poem text and pre-reading pictures)

periods.activity_title: Summary Completion and Central Idea Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.19): fill-in-blank poem summary using eight box words.
Let us discuss (p.19): complete two sentences — narrative style and central idea.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.19): pick three examples each for spider-effort lines and alliteration.

time_bands.activity: Invite two or three students to share a striking line they noticed during the read-aloud of the poem. This warms the class back into the poem's world before moving to written exercises.

Students work individually on the 'Let us discuss' fill-in-the-blank summary (p.19), choosing from the eight box words (tried, mounted, despair, attempts, great, conquered, low, strive). Once done, pairs compare and the teacher leads a whole-class confirmation.

Class discusses the two sentence-completion items from 'Let us discuss' (p.19) — why the poem uses a narrative style and what its central idea is. Teacher invites several formulations and guides the class toward a well-expressed statement.

periods.teacher_notes: The fill-in summary is the poem's story compressed into eight key words from the poem itself; students who re-read stanzas to locate the words are doing valuable close reading. A common difficulty is distinguishing 'low despair' from simple sadness — draw attention to the poem's opening stanzas where Bruce's mood is physical, not just emotional. The alliteration and spider-effort task is set for independent follow-up at home.
materials: Textbook p.19 ('Let us discuss' tasks I and II)

periods.activity_title: Literary Devices — Repetition, Simile and Metaphor

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.19): discuss why the poet repeats 'tried and tried', 'steadily, steadily', 'up, up'.
Let us discuss (p.20): identify metaphors and similes in nine given sentences.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.20–21): transform similes to metaphors and metaphors to similes.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to read aloud the three repeated phrases — 'tried and tried', 'steadily, steadily', 'up, up' — and discuss why Eliza Cook uses them. Teacher draws out how repetition enacts the persistence it describes, using the 'Let us discuss' prompt (p.19).

Briefly introduce the distinction between simile and metaphor, using the poem's own extended comparison of the spider's journey to Bruce's struggles as the anchor example before moving to the exercise.

Students work through the nine sentences from 'Let us discuss' (p.20), labelling each M or S individually, then share answers. Teacher clarifies any items where the class disagrees, focusing on the absence or presence of 'like' and 'as'.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often label all figurative comparisons as similes; the key move is showing that the spider in the poem is never said to be 'like' Bruce — the comparison is implied, making it a metaphor. The transformation exercise (converting similes to metaphors and vice versa) is set for independent follow-up and deepens the same skill at home.
materials: Textbook pp.19–21 ('Let us discuss' tasks IV and VI.1)

periods.activity_title: Close Reading of Extracts and Character Change

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.21): extract 1 questions — King's despair and 'silken filmy clue'.
Let us think and reflect (p.22): how the first stanza sets the mood and Bruce's attitude change.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 aloud ('He flung himself down in low despair…With its silken, filmy clue') and students work through the four questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.21): the physical expression of Bruce's mood, the effect of 'low', the meaning of 'pondered', and the image created by 'silken filmy clue'.

Move to the open questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.22): how the first stanza sets the poem's mood, and how Bruce's attitude changes from despair to resolve. Teacher invites extended responses and guides students to trace the shift across specific stanzas.

periods.teacher_notes: The physical vocabulary of despair — 'flung himself down', 'low despair' — is central to the poem's emotional arc; prompt students to contrast these images with the energetic vocabulary of the closing stanzas. A common pitfall is treating Bruce's final success as sudden inspiration rather than a gradual resolve that mirrors the spider's incremental climb. The extract-2 questions (pp.21–22) are not covered here and may serve as independent reading.
materials: Textbook pp.21–22 ('Let us think and reflect' tasks I Extract 1 and II)

periods.activity_title: Listening to the Ant Story and Personal Narration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.24): pre-listen prediction for five MCQ questions about the ant story.
Let us listen (p.24): listen to the story and verify predicted answers.
Let us speak (p.25): narrate a personal perseverance experience using seven guided prompts.

time_bands.activity: Students read the five prediction questions from 'Let us listen' (p.24) silently and write their guesses before hearing the story. This pre-listening task activates expectations and prepares focused attention.

Teacher reads the ant story aloud at a steady pace (p.40 transcript). Students listen carefully, then check their predicted answers against what they heard; the class discusses any surprises together.

Students prepare a brief personal narration using the seven prompts from 'Let us speak' (p.25) — introduction, challenge, disheartened moment, source of motivation, action taken, result, reflection. Two or three volunteers share with the class, with teacher feedback on fluency and structure.

periods.teacher_notes: The ant story closely parallels the poem's theme of perseverance and teamwork, so students making the connection aloud before speaking will give their narrations a richer frame. Encourage quieter students by inviting them to share just one prompt at a time rather than the full sequence. Students who do not get a turn to speak aloud may write a one-paragraph version as a brief independent task.
materials: Textbook pp.24–25 ('Let us listen' and 'Let us speak')

periods.activity_title: Planning and Drafting an Informal Letter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.26): plan and draft a letter to a cousin on overcoming difficulty with transition words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models an informal letter format on the board, showing the address, date, greeting and sign-off from the 'Let us write' prompt (p.26). Students identify the five transition words — 'To begin with', 'Next', 'After that', 'Then', 'Finally' — and note where each belongs in a plan.

Students outline their letter: what difficult situation they will describe, and the five steps they plan to take, mapped to the transition words. Teacher circulates and gives brief oral feedback on plans before students begin drafting.
Students draft the full letter to their cousin (p.26), using the given opening and closing lines. They aim to weave in advice about perseverance inspired by the spider's lesson from the poem.
Students swap letters with a partner for a quick peer read — checking that transition words are used and that the advice is clear. One or two students read a sentence they are proud of to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often forget that an informal letter to a cousin still needs an organised argument; the transition words scaffold this structure. The spider's lesson from the poem is the recommended source of inspiration for the advice, making the writing task a natural extension of the poem's meaning. Students who finish early can add a second paragraph with a personal example.

periods.activity_title: Word Meanings, Antonyms and Distance Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.22): write opposites of five poem words — up, fast, glad, win, succeed.
Let us learn (p.23): match meanings to four poem words and frame own sentences.
Let us learn (p.23): classify eleven distance words and phrases as far or near.

time_bands.activity: Students write the opposites of five words drawn from the poem — up, fast, glad, win, succeed — from 'Let us learn' (p.22). Quick whole-class check follows; teacher links the words back to the poem's emotional shifts.

Students match the four words (endeavour, toil, strive, braced) to their meanings from the box in 'Let us learn' (p.23), then frame an original sentence for each. Teacher invites two or three students to read their sentences aloud for peer response.

Students classify the eleven distance words and phrases (proximity, middle of nowhere, vicinity, adjacent, remoteness, yonder, afar, a stone's throw, light year, hairline, farther) into the Far/Near table from 'Let us learn' (p.23). Teacher connects this to the poem's own distance phrases such as 'inch by inch' and 'a long way up'.

periods.teacher_notes: The word 'endeavour' is used formally in the exercise sentence, which may seem distant from students' everyday vocabulary; grounding it in the spider's repeated attempts makes the meaning concrete. Students sometimes place 'hairline' and 'a stone's throw' in the wrong column — prompt them to think about what each phrase implies about the gap between two points. The tongue-twister task (Task IV, p.24) is not covered in class and can be explored independently.
materials: Textbook pp.22–23 ('Let us learn' tasks I, II and III)

periods.activity_title: Observing Nature and Weaving a Spider Web

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.26): observe a spider and ant image, note differences, share with class.
Let us explore (p.26–27): weave a spider web from sticks and wool, decorate with poem words.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.26): collect folk songs in your language connecting with nature for a class project.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly explains that spiders are arachnids, not insects, and asks students to look closely at the pictures of a spider and an ant (p.26) and note differences — number of legs, body segments, silk production. Pairs share observations; teacher adds any key distinctions students miss.

Students follow the four-step instructions from 'Let us explore' (p.26–27) to weave a spider web using three sticks and wool provided in class. Teacher demonstrates tying the centre knot and the looping technique; students work individually or in pairs.

Students write two or three words or phrases from the poem onto a slip of paper and attach them to their finished web — for example, 'steadily, steadily' or 'defied despair'. A quick gallery walk lets the class see each other's webs and word choices.

periods.teacher_notes: The spider-web craft works best when students have tied the centre knot firmly before beginning to loop the wool; demonstrate this step slowly. The spider-versus-ant observation connects the poem's extended metaphor to real biology, and students who recall the ant story from the listening activity will find natural links. The folk-song collection task is set as an ongoing project for independent work.
materials: Textbook pp.26–27 ('Let us explore' tasks II and III)
Three sticks (approx. 20 cm each) per student or pair
Rolls of wool or thick thread
Small paper slips and pens for word-decoration

items.source_lo: Student interprets meaning, mood and literary devices in a narrative poem using close reading and discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: King Bruce's despair, spider's nine attempts, repetition, ABAB rhyme, extended metaphor for perseverance.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 16 beginning "He flung himself down in low despair". Which option best describes the mood created in the opening stanzas of 'Try Again'?

options.label: A
options.text: Angry and resentful, as Bruce blames his people for his failure.

options.label: B
options.text: Curious and playful, as Bruce watches the spider for amusement.

options.label: C
options.text: Gloomy and defeated, as Bruce contemplates giving up his great deed.

options.label: D
options.text: Joyful and celebratory, as Bruce prepares for victory.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the poem's triumphant closing tone with its opening mood of despair.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Mistakes Bruce's distracted observation of the spider for lighthearted curiosity rather than desperate searching for hope.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a blame narrative not present in the poem; Bruce's despair is self-directed, not outward.

items.source_lo: Student interprets meaning, mood and literary devices in a narrative poem using close reading and discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: King Bruce's despair, spider's nine attempts, repetition, ABAB rhyme, extended metaphor for perseverance.
items.item_stem: Eliza Cook uses repetition as a key device in 'Try Again'. Consider the phrases "tried and tried", "up, up", and "steadily, steadily". Explain how this repeated language reflects the poem's central message about perseverance, and describe how it affects a reader following the spider's nine attempts.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The repeated phrases mimic the act of persistent effort itself — each repetition feels like another attempt, reinforcing that success requires the same action done again and again. A reader watching the spider make nine climbs experiences the mounting tension and exhaustion through the rhythm of repeated words before the final triumph.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short narrative, predicts and verifies information, and draws meaning from an oral text using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Ant story: determination, roti too heavy to carry alone, bird building nest inspires ant, teamwork succeeds.
items.item_stem: Listen to the story of the ant in the forest. Which of the following correctly states why the ant could not carry the piece of roti back to the anthill on her own?

options.label: A
options.text: Other ants blocked her path to the anthill.

options.label: B
options.text: The ant was tired from a long journey before finding the roti.

options.label: C
options.text: The piece of roti was too heavy for her to carry alone.

options.label: D
options.text: The roti was stuck under a heavy rock.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the obstacle with a physical barrier described in a different story context; the transcript mentions weight, not a rock.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a conflict between ants not present in the transcript; the fellow ants are helpers, not obstacles.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Adds a detail of prior fatigue not stated in the transcript; the ant's exhaustion comes from struggling with the roti, not a journey.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short narrative, predicts and verifies information, and draws meaning from an oral text using listen-and-respond as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Ant story: determination, roti too heavy to carry alone, bird building nest inspires ant, teamwork succeeds.
items.item_stem: In the ant story, a small bird also struggles — it keeps trying to build a nest even when the wind blows its twigs away. Explain what the ant learned by watching the bird, and describe how that lesson changed what the ant did next.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The ant saw that the bird refused to give up despite repeated setbacks, and this inspired her not to abandon her own struggle. Motivated by the bird's persistence, the ant called her fellow ants for help; together they formed a chain and successfully carried the roti back to the anthill.

items.item_stem: Describe a time when you faced a difficulty and felt like giving up. Tell your classmates what the challenge was and who or what gave you the push to keep going.

expected_elements: Names a specific challenge faced by the speaker.
Describes the moment of feeling disheartened clearly.
Identifies a source of motivation — person, event or observation.
Speaks in a connected sequence with a clear result.

items.item_stem: King Bruce chose to try again after watching the spider, even though he had already failed many times. If you were advising a friend who was about to give up on something important, what would you say to them, and why? Give your opinion with at least one reason drawn from your own experience or from what you know about persistence.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion about not giving up.
Supports the opinion with a personal example or observation.
Uses persuasive or empathetic language suited to advising a friend.
Reflects on why repeated effort has value beyond immediate success.

items.item_stem: Write a short informal letter to a younger cousin who is feeling discouraged about learning a new skill. In your letter, suggest at least three steps they could take to keep going. Use the transition words 'To begin with', 'Next' and 'Finally' to organise your advice. Remember to include an address, date, greeting and sign-off.

expected_elements: Includes correct informal letter format: address, date, greeting, sign-off.
Uses at least three transition words to sequence advice logically.
Offers concrete, actionable steps rather than vague encouragement.
Maintains a warm, encouraging tone appropriate for a younger cousin.

items.source_lo: Student composes a structured informal letter using transition words and functional letter format as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Informal letter to cousin advising on overcoming difficulty; spider-inspired perseverance; transition words sequencing steps.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are King Bruce writing a letter to a fellow king who has just suffered a great defeat and is thinking of giving up. In your letter, share what you witnessed — a small creature's determined climb — and explain in your own words why you believe one more attempt is worth making. You may write freely, without set transition words, but your letter must be organised and persuasive.

expected_elements: Adopts Bruce's voice convincingly with relevant detail from the poem.
Describes the spider's climb as the source of renewed resolve.
Constructs a persuasive argument for attempting once more.
Organises the letter with a clear opening, body and close.

items.item_stem: Match each word from the poem 'Try Again' in Column A with its closest meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
endeavour | to work very hard for a long time
toil | to try very hard to achieve something
strive | an attempt to do something difficult
braced | prepared for something hard

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: endeavour – an attempt to do something difficult; toil – to work very hard for a long time; strive – to try very hard to achieve something; braced – prepared for something hard.

answer_key.right: an attempt to do something difficult
to work very hard for a long time
to try very hard to achieve something

items.source_context: Antonyms of poem words; meanings of endeavour, toil, strive, braced; distance vocabulary — proximity, afar, adjacent, yonder.
items.item_stem:
The poem 'Try Again' is full of distance — the spider climbs from near the ground to the ceiling dome, 'inch by inch' and 'half-yard higher'. Choose the word from the box below that best completes each sentence, and explain in a sentence why your chosen word fits.

Box: afar  adjacent  proximity  yonder

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Possible answers: 'afar' fits a sentence describing something far away (like the ceiling dome from the spider's starting point); 'adjacent' fits something positioned very close or next to something; 'proximity' fits a reference to nearness (the spider inching close to its cobweb home); 'yonder' fits something visible but at a distance. Accept any well-reasoned sentence that correctly uses the distance meaning of the chosen word.

items.item_stem: Observe the images of a spider and an ant carefully. Note down at least three ways in which a spider is different from an ant. Present your observations to the class, connecting at least one difference to the spider's role in the poem 'Try Again'.

expected_elements: Lists at least three observable differences (e.g., eight legs vs six, body segments, silk production).
Uses accurate descriptive language for biological features.
Connects one biological feature — such as silk spinning — to the poem's imagery.
Presents observations in a clear, organised sequence.

items.item_stem: Create a spider web using three sticks and wool, following the four steps described in 'Let us explore'. Once your web is complete, choose five words or phrases from the poem 'Try Again' that best capture the spider's journey, and attach them to your web. Write a short caption (two or three sentences) explaining why you chose those particular words.

expected_elements: Produces a completed web following the four construction steps.
Selects five words or phrases clearly drawn from the poem.
Caption explains the connection between chosen words and the spider's actions.
Demonstrates understanding of how language in the poem builds meaning.
